title: Mapel (man's ceremonial skirt)
region: Kuba peoples, Democratic Republic of the Congo
altText: A long, narrow textile made of raffia fiber with geometric patterns across its surface. It is about 3.8 meters long and 74 centimeters wide.

context: A ceremonial wrapper, called a mapel, made by a Kuba artist in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the mid to late 19th century. The record lists raffia palm fiber, cotton, and dye. It is very long, about 376 centimeters, and about 74 centimeters wide. Kuba textiles from raffia fiber are known for their geometric patterns.

descriptions.k: This is a long cloth made from palm leaf fibers. Kuba artists in Central Africa made it by hand. It is covered in patterns. Can you find lines, zigzags, or boxes? It is longer than a grown-up is tall!
descriptions.g12: This long cloth was made by Kuba artists in Central Africa. It is woven from the fibers of a raffia palm tree. It is almost four meters long, longer than two grown-ups lying head to toe! Look for patterns made with lines and shapes. Which pattern do you like best?
descriptions.g35: Kuba artists in the Democratic Republic of the Congo made this ceremonial skirt, called a mapel, in the 1800s. It is woven from raffia palm fibers and decorated with geometric patterns. It is about 376 centimeters long, much longer than a person is tall, so it was wrapped around the body. Look for shapes that repeat and shapes that change. How does the artist make so many patterns work together?
descriptions.g68: Kuba textiles are admired for their geometric patterns and their raffia fiber, which is taken from palm leaves. This mapel is a man's ceremonial skirt made in the mid to late 19th century, and at about 376 centimeters long it was made to be wrapped and layered. Kuba cloth is commonly described as a team effort, with men weaving the raffia and women adding embroidery and dye, although the museum record names no individual maker. How do pattern, scale, and repetition make this long cloth feel like a single design?
descriptions.g910: This 19th-century Kuba mapel shows how raffia, a plant fiber, becomes a ground for complex pattern. Kuba cloth is often made in a shared process: raffia is woven, then dyed, embroidered, or appliquéd. Ceremonial textiles like this one marked occasions and status, but the record does not specify how this cloth was used or which patterns have names. The great length of the cloth, over three and a half meters, means that it was meant to be worn in folds and layers. How might a design change when it is seen on a moving body rather than laid flat?
descriptions.g1112: Kuba textiles occupy an important place in discussions of African art because their patterned surfaces have long been compared to modern abstraction, a comparison that can both open and limit our understanding. This mapel, a ceremonial wrapper of raffia, cotton, and dye, comes from a society in which cloth was used to mark rank and occasion, but the record gives limited information about its maker or its use. Its length of over three and a half meters implies a garment worn in layers and folds. How can we appreciate the formal inventiveness of the pattern while keeping the focus on its role in Kuba life?

teacherNote.context: A Kuba ceremonial wrapper (mapel) from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, mid to late 19th century, made of raffia palm fiber, cotton, and dye. The record names no individual maker or pattern names, so avoid presenting interpretations as fact.
directions: Have students design a long strip of paper with a repeating pattern that includes one deliberate change.
Trace a long strip of string across the classroom to feel the length of the mapel (about 3.8 meters).
Discuss how patterns can be admired for their design while still respecting that the makers had their own meanings for them.
